name: Zachery Pipes
title: Software Engineer
summary: Computer Science student at Missouri S&T (3.7 GPA, graduating Fall 2027). Focused on performance-oriented and systems-level software. Leads special projects for the S&T Multirotor Design Team, building Unreal Engine drone flight simulations and mentoring incoming members. Planning to pursue a Master's in Computer Science after graduating.

bullets: Directed three engineering sub-teams (9+ members) spanning flight simulation, developer tooling, and 3D terrain mapping

Led migration of the team simulator from legacy AirSim to Project AirSim, containerizing the Unreal Engine and ArduPilot SITL stack (Podman/WSL2) and restructuring it as a shared submodule serving the design team's competition codebases
Cut new-member setup from a multi-hour source build to a single pull by publishing prebuilt environment and SITL images to GitHub Container Registry behind a one-command launcher
Structured sub-team work around end-to-end feature ownership rather than by layer, giving every member hands-on work with the team's core technologies
Led onboarding for 5+ new members, training them in Python, Git submodule workflows, and containerized development environments
Developed C++ software for a UAV platform, contributing through code review and testing
Collaborated with 10+ teammates in a student-led UAV startup advancing next-generation UAV technology under active NDA
Modeled product components in Blender and produced marketing renders used in the company website and pitch decks
Evaluated candidate UAV components against Blue UAS sourcing requirements, weighing compliance against performance constraints
Processed and shipped packages to destinations across the United States
Trained new employees on store procedures and best practices
Provided excellent customer service through answering questions, resolving issues, and providing solutions tailored to customer needs,

projects.name: fastdist
bullets: Implemented 26 CUDA kernels accelerating 5 probability distributions and vector utilities, with a streaming executor that splits large inputs across 4 concurrent CUDA streams

Built the pybind11/NumPy wrapper layer between C++ and Python, releasing the GIL during computation and managing GPU memory through self-freeing buffer objects that are allocated once and reused across calls, replacing manual cleanup on six separate error paths
Achieved up to 57x speedup over SciPy with the C++ CPU backend alone, with CUDA kernels adding a further 2.5x over the CPU path on large inputs

Automated cross-platform wheel builds for Linux, macOS (x86_64/arm), and Windows across Python 3.10--3.14, with trusted-publishing releases to PyPI and a CI check that catches type-stub drift against a CUDA build
